title: KS3 Geography - Energy Resources

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Energy Resources
data.sourcePassage: Energy is needed for heating, cooking, transport, industry, communication and public services. In Geography, energy is not only about how power is made. It is also about places, people, decisions and impacts. Countries use different energy resources depending on their physical geography, wealth, technology, politics and links with other countries. An energy resource can be a fuel, such as coal, oil or gas, or a natural force, such as sunlight, wind or moving water. Every energy choice creates trade-offs. A wind farm can produce low-carbon electricity, but some people may dislike its appearance or worry about wildlife. A gas power station can respond quickly to demand, but it releases greenhouse gases. Strong geographical answers compare cost, reliability, carbon emissions, land use, safety, jobs and long-term sustainability.

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Energy Resources
data.sourceTitle: Fossil Fuels, Nuclear Power and Climate
data.targetTitle: Fossil Fuels, Nuclear Power and Climate
data.sourcePassage: Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels. They formed from ancient living material that was buried, heated and compressed over millions of years. Fossil fuels are non-renewable because they are used much faster than they are naturally replaced. Coal can generate large amounts of electricity, but it has very high carbon emissions and can cause air pollution. Oil is especially useful for transport fuels, but oil spills can damage marine and coastal ecosystems. Natural gas produces less carbon dioxide than coal for the same amount of electricity, but it still releases greenhouse gases and imported gas can create energy security risks. Nuclear power is different. It is not a fossil fuel and it has low operational carbon emissions, but uranium is limited and radioactive waste must be stored safely for a very long time.

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Energy Resources
data.sourcePassage: Renewable energy sources are naturally replaced on a human timescale. Solar power uses sunlight and works best in sunny places, although it can still work in the UK. Wind power uses moving air to turn turbines; the UK has strong offshore wind potential because it has windy seas and a long coastline. Hydroelectric power uses moving water and is most suitable where there are wet, steep rivers. Tidal power is predictable because tides rise and fall regularly, but only some coasts are suitable. Geothermal energy works best where heat from inside the Earth is close to the surface, such as Iceland with its volcanic activity. Renewable energy usually has low carbon emissions during operation, but renewable does not mean no impact. Dams can flood valleys, turbines can affect views or wildlife, and solar farms need land and materials.

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Energy Resources
data.sourcePassage: Energy demand is the amount of energy people, businesses or countries want to use. Demand can rise because of population growth, economic development, more transport, industry, technology, heating and cooling. Demand can fall when buildings become more efficient, industries change or people waste less energy. An energy mix is the percentage of energy from different sources. Countries usually use a mixture because each source has strengths and weaknesses. Energy security means having a reliable and affordable supply of energy. Insecurity can happen when a country imports lots of fuel, prices rise suddenly, pipelines are disrupted, infrastructure is old or extreme weather damages energy systems. Solutions include improving efficiency, using a balanced energy mix, storing fuel, investing in smart grids and developing local renewable energy.

data.chapter: KS3 Geography Study Pack: Energy Resources
data.sourcePassage: Sustainable energy means meeting current energy needs without causing serious problems for future generations. It usually combines reducing demand, improving efficiency and using more low-carbon or renewable energy. Home insulation reduces heating demand and bills, although it can have an upfront cost. LED lighting and efficient appliances reduce electricity use. Public transport, cycling and walking can cut transport energy demand. Smart grids help balance supply and demand, especially when solar and wind output changes. Batteries can store electricity for later use, but their materials, cost and recycling need managing. A strong energy strategy rarely depends on one source. For example, a small island with strong winds, a rocky coast and expensive imported diesel might reduce demand first, then use offshore wind and possibly tidal power, while keeping some backup for emergencies.
